APRP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every April.
AUGP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each August, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every August.
BBLB: US Treasury bonds with more than twenty years left until they mature, and nothing else. It is a pure bet on long-term interest rates: prices jump when rates fall and drop hard when rates rise, and it can act as a cushion when stocks sell off sharply.
BESF: Actively managed US energy stocks: oil and gas producers, pipeline operators and energy service companies make up nearly the whole fund. It is a focused bet on the energy industry, used for its income and its link to fuel prices, and it swings with the price of oil and gas.
CCFE: A concentrated, actively managed set of small US companies the managers judge cheap relative to their worth, leaning heavily on industrial and consumer businesses. It is a focused value bet, so it can trail badly when small, out-of-favor stocks lag, and it holds some cash while hunting for ideas.
DDTG: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from August, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTN: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from November, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTS: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from September, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTZ: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from June, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
FOPC: A fund of bond funds: roughly six to twelve other ETFs spanning US fixed income, chosen and shifted by its managers in search of extra yield. It plays a flexible core-plus bond role, reaching into credit corners a plain investment grade fund skips, which adds both income and risk.
GENM: Intermediate municipal bonds rated A or better, issued by states, cities and public agencies across the US. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, so it is an income holding aimed at investors in higher tax brackets who want quality and a middle-of-the-road maturity.
GK: Actively managed growth stocks picked around long-running investment themes, with technology about 44 percent, plus industrial, media and health care names. It is a growth holding run on the managers' judgment rather than an index, so its fortunes depend heavily on the themes they favor at the time.
HEAL: Companies building health technology: digital health platforms, medical data, connected devices and software that modernize how care is delivered and paid for. It is a focused growth bet on the digital side of health care rather than drugmakers, so it swings with sentiment toward young tech companies.
HEQQ: Big Nasdaq-listed companies, heavy in technology at about 60 percent, combined with a laddered options overlay that hedges part of the market risk. It aims to keep much of the growth of tech-led stocks while softening falls, trading away some upside for a smoother ride than the unhedged index.
HOMZ: One hundred companies across the US housing chain: homebuilders, housing real estate trusts, building suppliers and home improvement retailers. It is a focused bet on American housing, so it rises and falls with homebuilding, mortgage rates and the property market rather than the stock market as a whole.
HXC: A broad basket of commodities, from energy and metals to farm goods, held through futures and related contracts rather than physical goods. It is built as a diversifier and inflation hedge whose returns come from commodity price moves, and its managers use hedging techniques to try to smooth the ride.
IBHL: High yield and other income-paying corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, so the fund behaves like a single bond with an end date. It is used to target income for a known future year, and when 2032 arrives the fund winds down and returns cash to holders.
IBIM: Inflation-protected Treasury bonds, known as TIPS, that mature around October 2036, so the fund has a set end date like a single bond. Its payments and principal adjust with inflation, making it a targeted way to protect a known future year's spending from rising prices.
IINC: Large and midsize US stocks paired with an options program that sells contracts on holdings to collect premium payments. The point is monthly style income from a stock portfolio, with the trade-off that selling options gives away part of the upside when share prices climb quickly.
JADE: Actively managed stocks across developing markets, from Asia to Latin America, with technology about 42 percent and banks about a quarter. It is a growth holding built on the managers' company research on the ground in those markets, and it carries the bigger swings emerging markets are known for.
JPO: A single-stock income strategy built on JPMorgan Chase shares, using options on that one banking giant to generate monthly payments. Because everything rides on one company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and the bank's drops hit directly.
JUNZ: Options on the big US stock index shape returns over a year starting each June, aiming to soften losses with a built-in buffer while keeping a share of gains up to a cap. It is a structured, defined-window stock holding, so when you buy relative to the June start matters.
KMAR: Small US companies reached through options on a small-cap fund, with a power buffer designed to absorb a larger slice of losses over a year starting each March. Small stocks swing more than large ones, so the extra protection is the point, and in exchange the gains are capped.
LDRI: A ladder built from several inflation-protected bond funds, each maturing in a different year within a one to five year span. It spreads TIPS exposure across near-term dates for inflation-adjusted income with modest price swings, and the ladder rolls forward as the nearest funds reach their end.
LKOR: Long-term US corporate bonds, all investment grade, screened by Northern Trust for sound credit, fair value and strong balance sheets. Picking quality long bonds is the twist: it aims for income with less credit risk than a plain long corporate fund, though long maturities still swing when rates move.
LUNC: A worldwide portfolio of what its managers call misclassified compounders: profitable companies they believe the market has filed in the wrong category. Unusually for a global fund, raw materials and energy together make up almost two thirds, so it behaves more like a resources fund than a broad world index.
MAYP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each May, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every May.
MHY: Actively managed high yield bonds: lower-rated corporate debt paying higher interest, in both fixed and floating rate forms. It is an income holding that takes real credit risk, so it tends to fall when investors worry about defaults, and the management team shifts holdings as conditions change.
NDIV: Energy and natural resource companies, mostly oil and gas producers and pipelines, wrapped in a covered call program that sells options on the holdings for extra income. It is built for high income from the energy sector, trading away some upside when fuel prices surge.
NVBT: Options on a fund of the largest US companies match its returns over one year from November, buffering the first 10 percent of losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms are set each November, so it is a defined-window holding for investors who want stock exposure with known protection.
OBND: A go-anywhere bond portfolio run by Loomis Sayles managers, spanning government, corporate, mortgage and other debt, with room for preferred and convertible securities. It is a flexible income holding that leans on manager judgment to hunt for value across bond markets, including through other funds.
OCTM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each October. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
OCTP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to stay invested in stocks with some protection when markets fall.
PAWZ: Companies that earn from pet ownership: animal health and drug makers, pet food brands, retailers and veterinary services. It is a focused bet on steady spending on pets, mixing health care, consumer staples and shops, so it moves with that industry rather than the broad market.
PAYH: Exposure to an index built from autocallable notes, structured products that pay high coupons as long as markets behave and can end early when conditions are met. It chases high income, and the notes are linked to a volatility measure, so sharp market stress can cut both income and principal.
PEMX: Actively picked companies across emerging markets, with China and Hong Kong left out entirely, so chipmakers and banks in Taiwan, South Korea and India dominate and technology is over half the fund. It is a growth holding for investors who want developing markets without the China exposure most such funds carry.
PQAP: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
RFFC: Actively managed US stocks across all major industries, with technology the largest slice at about a third, chosen by managers hunting for opportunities rather than copying an index. It is a flexible core style holding whose results depend on stock picking, and it can hold real estate trusts too.
RSDE: Exposure to an equal weight version of the big US stock index, where every company counts the same, wrapped in options that buffer a slice of losses over a year starting each December. Smaller index members matter more here than in the usual market-weighted funds, and gains are capped.
SALI: Income from a ladder of autocallable notes reached through swap contracts: structured notes linked to stock indexes that pay coupons and can end early when markets rise. Laddering staggers the notes' dates, and the fund aims for high regular income, with returns tied to how those notes perform.
SCSB: Short-term, mostly investment grade bonds from governments, companies and municipalities, with a small allowance for lower-rated debt. It is built for income with modest price swings, since short maturities react less when interest rates move, though its yield is lower than riskier bond funds offer.
SEPP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each September, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every September.
TIIV: Large companies outside the US, bought as ADRs and foreign shares, with banks the biggest slice at about a third, then industrial and technology firms. Managers hunt for stocks priced below what the business seems worth, so it plays the patient value role in an international stock holding.
TJAN: Built from options on the S&P 500 to protect against the full loss of the underlying fund over a two-year outcome period ending in January 2027, in exchange for a cap on gains. The defined protection is the point: it trades away the top of the market to take the bottom off it.
TPUT: An options-based strategy that adjusts how much stock market exposure it takes, holding Treasury securities and cash-like assets as collateral and an income source while conditions are calm. It aims for capital growth with a disciplined, rules-driven options program, and it can sit largely in safe assets at times.
VDIG: Large US companies chosen by Wellington managers for their record and prospects of growing dividends, spread across technology, finance and health care. It is a core style stock holding aiming for income that rises over time plus steady growth, favoring established payers over the fastest growers.
VSHY: High yield corporate bonds with short maturities, so the higher interest of below-investment-grade debt comes with less sensitivity to interest rate moves. It is an income holding for investors who want junk bond yields but a somewhat steadier ride, though defaults remain the main risk in downturns.
WBIG: A tactical mix of US and foreign stocks of all sizes picked for value and dividend yield, plus bond funds and a large cash cushion that shifts with conditions. It aims for income with active risk control, moving defensive when its managers see trouble, so results hinge on their calls.
XNAV: A fund of other ETFs that leans aggressively into whichever stock sectors and growth funds are showing strength, so technology-heavy funds can dominate. It is a momentum style growth holding that shifts its mix over time, accepting concentrated bets and bigger swings in pursuit of stronger returns.
ZHDG: US stocks combined with options hedges and income-producing securities in a buy-and-hedge design meant to keep a portion of stock gains while cushioning declines. The hedging trades some upside for protection, so it aims for a steadier path than an unprotected stock fund through rough markets.
